Physics I (8.01)

Introduction

Study of physics is:

  • classical mechanics
  • relativity
  • thermodynamics
  • electromagnetism
  • optics
  • quantum mechanics

Units

SI units:

Base quantity SI Symbol Defining constant
Time second s \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{Cs}}
Length metre m c
Mass kilogram kg h
Electric current ampere A e
Thermodynamic temperature kelvin K k_{\mathrm B}
Amount of substance mole mol N_{\mathrm A}
Luminous intensity candela cd K_{\mathrm{cd}}

Defining constants:

  • \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{Cs}}: caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency fixed at 9\,192\,631\,770\,\mathrm{Hz}; defines the second.
  • c: speed of light in vacuum fixed at 299\,792\,458\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}; defines the metre from the second.
  • h: Planck constant fixed at 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}; defines the kilogram using the metre and second.
  • e: elementary charge fixed at 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}; defines the ampere using the second.
  • k_{\mathrm B}: Boltzmann constant fixed at 1.380649 \times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}; links temperature to energy.
  • N_{\mathrm A}: Avogadro constant fixed at 6.02214076 \times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}; one mole contains exactly this many specified entities.
  • K_{\mathrm{cd}}: luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{Hz} fixed at 683\,\mathrm{lm\,W^{-1}}.

Measurement

Measured quantities are known only up to experimental uncertainty:

x=(a\pm\Delta a)\times10^n, \quad \Delta x=10^n\Delta a.

For worst-case error bounds,

z=x\pm y\implies\Delta z\leq\Delta x+\Delta y, \quad z=xy\ \text{or}\ z=\frac{x}{y} \implies \frac{\Delta z}{|z|} \lesssim \frac{\Delta x}{|x|}+\frac{\Delta y}{|y|}.

For independent standard uncertainties, to first order,

z=x\pm y\implies\sigma_z=\sqrt{\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2}, \quad z=xy\ \text{or}\ z=\frac{x}{y} \implies \frac{\sigma_z}{|z|} \simeq \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\sigma_x}{|x|}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{\sigma_y}{|y|}\right)^2 }.

For z=f(x_1,x_2,\ldots),

\sigma_z^2 \simeq \sum_i \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \right)^2\sigma_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j} \operatorname{Cov}(x_i,x_j)

where the derivatives are evaluated at the measured values. For independent inputs, the covariance terms vanish.

Kinematics and Dynamics

Position, Velocity, Acceleration

A unit vector, e.g., \hat i, is a dimensionless vector having a magnitude of exactly 1.

Position: \vec r(t)=x(t)\hat i+y(t)\hat j+z(t)\hat k

Velocity: \vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dt} \hat{i} + \frac{dy}{dt} \hat{j} + \frac{dz}{dt} \hat{k} = \dot x \hat i + \dot y \hat j + \dot z \hat k

Speed:

v = |\vec v|

Acceleration: \vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \ddot{x} \hat{i} + \ddot{y} \hat{j} + \ddot{z} \hat{k}

The Laws of Motion

The four known fundamental interactions are the gravitational, electromagnetic, strong, and weak interactions:

  • gravitational forces between objects
  • electromagnetic forces between electric charges
  • strong forces between subatomic particles
  • weak forces that arise in certain radioactive decay processes

In introductory classical mechanics, the forces encountered are ultimately associated mainly with gravitational and electromagnetic interactions.

Newton’s first law

If an object does not interact with other objects, it is possible to identify a reference frame in which the object has zero acceleration.

More practically:

In the absence of external forces and when viewed from an inertial reference frame, an object at rest remains at rest and an object in motion continues in motion with a constant velocity (that is, with a constant speed in a straight line).

Newton’s second law

\sum \vec F_{\text{ext}} = \frac {\mathrm d \vec p}{\mathrm d t} = \frac{\mathrm d (m \vec v)}{\mathrm d t} = m \vec a \; \text{ for constant } m \qquad{(1)}

Newton’s third law

If two objects interact, the force \vec{\mathbf{F}}_{12} exerted by object 1 on object 2 is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force \vec{\mathbf{F}}_{21} exerted by object 2 on object 1:

\vec{\mathbf{F}}_{12}=-\vec{\mathbf{F}}_{21}

Frames

Newton’s laws of motion describe observations made in an inertial frame of reference.

In a rotating, noninertial reference frame, the centrifugal force is an apparent force directed radially outward from the axis of rotation. Unlike an interaction force, it has no corresponding source object; it arises from the acceleration of the reference frame. In an inertial reference frame, no centrifugal force acts, and the circular motion is instead explained by an inward centripetal force.

Energy and Momentum

Work

W_\text{net}=\lim_{|\Delta \vec r_i|\to 0}\sum_i\vec F_\text{net}\cdot\Delta\vec r_i=\int_C\vec F_\text{net}\cdot\mathrm d\vec r

Kinetic Work-Energy Theorem

For 1-D motion with constant mass:

\begin{aligned} & a\mathrm d x = \frac {\mathrm d v} {\mathrm d t} \mathrm d x = \frac {\mathrm d v} {\mathrm d x} \frac {\mathrm d x} {\mathrm d t} \mathrm d x = \frac {\mathrm d v} {\mathrm d x} v \mathrm d x = v \mathrm d v \\ \implies & W=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}ma\,\mathrm dx = \int_{v_i}^{v_f}mv\,dv=\frac{1}{2}mv_f^2-\frac{1}{2}mv_i^2 \\ \implies & K = \frac 1 2 m v^2 \\ \implies & \boxed{W_{net} = \Delta K} \end{aligned} \qquad{(2)}

Conservative Field

For a conservative force field \vec F with scalar potential energy U, \vec F = - \nabla U:

Assume this force is the only force doing work.

\begin{aligned} & W_{a\to b} = \Delta K=\int_{C:a\to b} \vec F \cdot \mathrm d \vec r = -[U(\vec r(b)) - U(\vec r(a))] = -\Delta U \\ \implies & \Delta (K + U) = 0 \end{aligned}

Linear Momentum

\vec p = m \vec v

Whenever two or more particles in an isolated system interact, the total momentum of the system remains constant.

Impulse

\vec{J} = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec{F} \mathrm d t \overset{\href{#eq:newton-second-law}{\text{(1)}}}{=} \int \frac {\mathrm d \vec p}{\mathrm d t}\mathrm d t = \Delta \vec p

Rotation

Position, Velocity, Acceleration

\omega=\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt}=\dot\theta,\quad \alpha=\frac{\mathrm d\omega}{\mathrm dt}=\ddot\theta

For circular motion with constant R:

\begin{aligned} \omega = & \frac {\mathrm d \theta}{\mathrm d t} = \dot \theta, \quad \vec v = \dot{\theta} \, R \hat \theta \\ \alpha = & \frac {\mathrm d \omega}{\mathrm d t} = \ddot \theta, \quad \vec a=-R\omega^2\hat r+R\alpha\hat\theta \end{aligned}

Moment of Inertia

\begin{aligned} I & = \int r_\perp^2 \, \mathrm dm \\ K_{\text{rot}} & = \int \mathrm d K = \int \frac{1}{2} \,(\mathrm d m)\, r_\perp^2\,\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}\,\omega^2 \int r_\perp^2 \, \mathrm dm = \frac 1 2 I \omega ^ 2 \\ \end{aligned}

Torque

\vec \tau = \vec r \times \vec F

The magnitude of the torque exerted by a force \vec F about a point is:

|\vec\tau_{\vec F}| =|\vec r\times\vec F| =rF\sin\phi =Fd

Figure 1 shows the perpendicular moment arm d=r\sin\phi from the pivot to the force’s line of action.

Work–Energy Theorem

Similar to Equation 2, for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with constant moment of inertia I:

\begin{aligned} & \alpha\,\mathrm d\theta = \frac{\mathrm d\omega}{\mathrm dt}\,\mathrm d\theta = \frac{\mathrm d\omega}{\mathrm d\theta}\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm dt}\,\mathrm d\theta = \omega\,\mathrm d\omega \\ \implies & W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K _{\text{rot}} = \int_{\theta_i}^{\theta_f}\tau_{\text{net}}\,\mathrm d\theta = \int_{\theta_i}^{\theta_f}I\alpha\,\mathrm d\theta = \int_{\omega_i}^{\omega_f}I\omega\,\mathrm d\omega = \frac{1}{2}I\omega_f^2-\frac{1}{2}I\omega_i^2 \\ \implies & K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \end{aligned}

Angular Momentum

The law of conservation of angular momentum is a fundamental law of physics, equally valid for relativistic and quantum systems.

\vec \tau = \vec r \times \vec F = \vec r \times \frac {\mathrm d \vec p} {\mathrm d t} \overset{\vec v \parallel \vec p}{=} \vec r \times \frac {\mathrm d \vec p} {\mathrm d t} + \vec v \times \vec p = \vec r \times \frac {\mathrm d \vec p} {\mathrm d t} + \frac{\mathrm d \vec r}{\mathrm d t} \times \vec p = \frac {\mathrm d (\vec r \times \vec p)}{\mathrm d t}

For a particle of mass m located at \vec r with linear momentum \vec p = m \vec v:

\vec L = \vec r \times \vec p \implies \vec \tau = \frac {\mathrm d \vec L}{\mathrm d t} = \vec r \times \vec F

For a rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis:

\begin{aligned} L_{\text{rot}} &= \int \omega r_\perp^2\mathrm d m = \omega I \\ \sum \tau & = \frac{\mathrm d L_{\text{rot}}}{\mathrm d t} = I \frac {\mathrm d \omega}{\mathrm d t} = I \alpha \end{aligned}

Equilibrium and Elasticity

Static Equilibrium

A body is in static equilibrium when it is at rest and remains at rest in an inertial frame. Its linear momentum and angular momentum do not change, so

\boxed{ \sum \vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}=\vec 0, \quad \sum \vec\tau_{O,\mathrm{ext}}=\vec 0 }

For a conservative system, an equilibrium q_0 satisfies

\left.\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dq}\right|_{q_0}=0

A local minimum of U is stable.

Stress and Strain

For simple, uniform deformation, stress is force per unit area and strain is relative deformation:

\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\frac{F_\perp}{A}, &\epsilon&=\frac{\Delta L}{L} &&\text{normal}, \\ \tau&=\frac{F_\parallel}{A}, &\gamma&\simeq\frac{\Delta x}{h} &&\text{shear}, \\ \Delta p&=\frac{\Delta F_\perp}{A}, &\epsilon_V&=\frac{\Delta V}{V} &&\text{volume} \end{aligned}

Stress has units of pascals; strain is dimensionless. Figure 2 shows the corresponding geometry.

Elastic Moduli

Within the linear elastic range, stress is proportional to strain:

\begin{aligned} E&=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} &&\text{Young's modulus}, \\ G&=\frac{\tau}{\gamma} &&\text{shear modulus}, \\ B&=-\frac{\Delta p}{\epsilon_V} =-\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta V/V} =-V\frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm dV} &&\text{bulk modulus} \end{aligned} \qquad{(3)}

The minus sign makes B>0 under compression.

Under uniaxial stress, Poisson’s ratio is

\nu=-\frac{\epsilon_\perp}{\epsilon_\parallel}

For an isotropic, linearly elastic material, only two of E, G, B, and \nu are independent:

E=2G(1+\nu), \quad E=3B(1-2\nu), \quad E=\frac{9BG}{3B+G}

A fluid at rest has G=0 but may have B>0. Outside the linear elastic range, these relations do not hold.

See the Elastic Moduli for step-by-step derivations.

Elastic Energy

For linear loading, the stored energy density is

\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{normal}} &=\frac12\sigma\epsilon =\frac12E\epsilon^2, \\ u_{\mathrm{shear}} &=\frac12\tau\gamma =\frac12G\gamma^2, \\ u_{\mathrm{volume}} &=-\frac12\Delta p\,\epsilon_V =\frac12B\epsilon_V^2 =\frac{(\Delta p)^2}{2B} \end{aligned}

Gravitation

Universal Gravitation

Let \hat r point from a point mass M to a second point mass m, with separation r. The gravitational force on m is

\vec F_{M\to m} =-G\frac{Mm}{r^2}\hat r, \quad G\approx6.67430 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}

Gravitational Field

The gravitational field generated by M is the force per unit mass:

\vec g_M(\vec r) =\frac{\vec F_{M\to m}}{m} =-G\frac{M}{r^2}\hat r

Define gravitational potential as potential energy per unit mass, so that \vec g_M=-\nabla\Phi_M. With \Phi_M(\infty)=0, a point mass produces

\Phi_M(r)=-\frac{GM}{r}

The gravitational potential energy of the pair M,m is

U=m\Phi_M=-\frac{GMm}{r}

Thus \Phi_M has units of energy per unit mass, while U is the pair’s gravitational potential energy.

Kepler’s Laws

For two isolated point masses, define the relative position and gravitational parameter by

\mathbf r=\mathbf r_m-\mathbf r_M, \quad \mu_g=G(M+m)

Newton’s laws reduce the two-body problem to the relative equation

\ddot{\mathbf r} =-\frac{\mu_g}{r^3}\mathbf r

For a collision-free orbit with nonzero angular momentum, this central force conserves the specific angular momentum \mathbf h=\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}, giving constant areal velocity. Its inverse-square radial dependence produces the conic orbit

r(\theta)=\frac{p}{1+e\cos(\theta-\omega)}

Here p is the semi-latus rectum, e is the eccentricity, \theta is the polar angle of \mathbf r, and \omega is the polar angle of periapsis.

With specific mechanical energy

\varepsilon =\frac12|\dot{\mathbf r}|^2-\frac{\mu_g}{r},

the orbit is bound if and only if \varepsilon<0, equivalently e<1.

  1. The relative orbit is a conic section with the inverse-square force center at one focus. A bound, collision-free orbit is an ellipse.

  2. The line joining the two bodies sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

  3. For a bound two-body orbit with semi-major axis a,

    T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{G(M+m)}a^3

For M\gg m, the third law reduces to T^2/a^3\approx4\pi^2/(GM).

See the Kepler’s Laws for a step-by-step derivation.

Fluid Mechanics

Pressure

Pressure is the normal force per unit area:

P=\frac{\mathrm dF_\perp}{\mathrm dA}

For a fluid at rest, with y measured upward, vertical force balance gives the hydrostatic relation

\frac{\mathrm dP}{\mathrm dy}=-\rho g

For constant density, the pressure at depth h below a surface where the pressure is P_0 is

P=P_0+\rho gh

The difference P-P_0=\rho gh is the gauge pressure relative to the surface.

Archimedes’ Principle

A body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid at rest experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid:

F_B=\rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{displaced}}g

Fluid Dynamics

For the elementary Bernoulli model used below, we assume that the flow is:

  • Nonviscous (inviscid): Viscous shear stresses and internal friction are neglected.
  • Steady: The velocity at each fixed point does not change with time, so \partial\vec v/\partial t=0.
  • Incompressible: The density of each fluid parcel remains constant; here we take \rho to be constant.

Irrotationality is an additional condition. For a fluid velocity field \vec v, its curl is called the vorticity:

\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\vec v

The local angular velocity of a fluid element is \boldsymbol\omega/2. A flow with \boldsymbol\omega=\vec 0 is irrotational. An infinitesimal paddle wheel carried by such a flow therefore has no local mean rotation.

For steady, incompressible, nonviscous flow under gravity, Bernoulli’s equation holds along a streamline. If the flow is also irrotational, the same Bernoulli constant applies throughout a connected flow region.

Bernoulli’s Equation

Consider a parcel of incompressible fluid moving through a streamtube from section 1 to section 2, as shown in Figure 3. During a short time interval \Delta t, the fluid advances by

\Delta x_1=v_1\Delta t, \quad \Delta x_2=v_2\Delta t

Because the flow is steady and incompressible, the same volume \Delta V crosses both sections:

\Delta V=A_1\Delta x_1=A_2\Delta x_2, \quad A_1v_1=A_2v_2

The upstream fluid does positive work P_1A_1\Delta x_1 on the parcel, while the downstream fluid does negative work -P_2A_2\Delta x_2. Thus the net pressure work is

W_P=P_1\Delta V-P_2\Delta V

For a parcel of mass \Delta m=\rho\Delta V, the work–energy theorem gives

\begin{aligned} P_1\Delta V-P_2\Delta V &=\Delta K+\Delta U \\ &=\frac12\rho\Delta V\left(v_2^2-v_1^2\right) +\rho g\Delta V\left(y_2-y_1\right). \end{aligned}

Dividing by \Delta V and collecting the terms associated with each section yields Bernoulli’s equation:

\boxed{ P_1+\frac12\rho v_1^2+\rho gy_1 =P_2+\frac12\rho v_2^2+\rho gy_2 }

Equivalently, along a streamline in steady, incompressible, nonviscous flow,

P+\frac12\rho v^2+\rho gy=\text{constant}

Each term has units of pressure, or energy per unit volume. The equation expresses a tradeoff among static pressure P, kinetic energy density \tfrac12\rho v^2, and gravitational potential energy density \rho gy.

Thermodynamics

Temperature

Ideal Gas Law

At low density, many gases obey

PV=nRT=Nk_{\mathrm B}T, \qquad{(4)}

where N=nN_{\mathrm A} and

R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}\approx(6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}})(1.381\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})\approx8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}

Special cases are:

  • Fixed T: PV=\text{constant} (Boyle’s law).
  • Fixed P: V/T=\text{constant} (Charles’s law).
  • Fixed V: P/T=\text{constant} (pressure law).

Expansion

For a small temperature change, linear expansion is

\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T,

where \alpha is the linear expansion coefficient.

Volume expansion is

\Delta V=\beta V_0\Delta T

For an isotropic solid, first-order expansion gives \beta\simeq3\alpha.

First Law

Internal Energy

Internal energy U is the microscopic kinetic and potential energy measured in the center-of-mass frame.

  • U is a state function: \Delta U depends only on the endpoint states.
  • Q is energy transferred into the system as heat.
  • W is energy transferred out as work done by the system.
  • Bulk kinetic and potential energies are not part of U.

With Q>0 into the system and W>0 out of the system, the first law is

\boxed{\Delta U=Q-W}

For a small change,

\mathrm dU=\delta Q-\delta W \qquad{(5)}

  • \mathrm dU is an exact differential.
  • \delta Q and \delta W are path-dependent transfers.

Heat Capacity

For a specified process, heat capacity is

C=\frac{\delta Q}{\mathrm dT}

If the specific heat c is constant and no phase change occurs,

Q=mc\Delta T

For calorimetry in an isolated enclosure,

\sum_i Q_i=0

Phase Change

At fixed pressure, a phase change can occur at constant temperature:

Q=\pm mL

  • L: latent heat per unit mass.
  • Q>0: energy enters the system.
  • Q<0: energy leaves the system.

PV Work

For a quasistatic piston displacement,

\delta W=F\,\mathrm dx=PA\,\mathrm dx=P\,\mathrm dV

Thus the work from volume V_i to V_f is

W=\int_{V_i}^{V_f}P\,\mathrm dV

  • Expansion: \mathrm dV>0 and \delta W>0.
  • Compression: \mathrm dV<0 and \delta W<0.
  • On a PV diagram, W is the signed area under the path.
  • W depends on the path; \Delta U depends only on the endpoints.

Heat Transfer

Heat transfer occurs through conduction, convection, and thermal radiation. The transfer rate is written \dot Q=\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt.

Conduction

For steady one-dimensional conduction through a uniform slab of thickness L, area A, and thermal conductivity k,

\dot Q=kA\frac{T_h-T_c}{L}=\frac{T_h-T_c}{R_{\mathrm{th}}}, \quad R_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac{L}{kA}

  • Series: R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_iR_i.
  • Parallel: R_{\mathrm{eq}}^{-1}=\sum_iR_i^{-1}.
  • Building R-value: R=L/k, so R_{\mathrm{th}}=R/A.

Convection

Convection transfers energy between a surface and a moving fluid. Newton’s law of cooling models the rate as

\dot Q=hA(T_s-T_f),

where the heat-transfer coefficient h depends on the fluid, geometry, and flow.

Radiation

Every body emits electromagnetic radiation. A body of surface area A, absolute temperature T, and emissivity \varepsilon radiates at the rate

P_{\mathrm{emit}}=\varepsilon\sigma AT^4,

where \sigma is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. If the surroundings act as a large enclosure at temperature T_{\mathrm{env}}, the net outward rate is

P_{\mathrm{net}}=\varepsilon\sigma A \left(T^4-T_{\mathrm{env}}^4\right)

Kinetic Theory

Pressure

The ideal-gas model assumes:

  • N identical molecules move randomly and obey Newtonian mechanics;
  • the molecular size is negligible compared with the container volume;
  • intermolecular forces are negligible except during brief elastic collisions;
  • collisions with one another and with the walls are elastic.

In a cube of side L, one molecule transfers momentum 2m|v_x| to an x-wall every 2L/|v_x|:

F_x=\frac{2m|v_x|}{2L/|v_x|}=\frac{mv_x^2}{L}

Summing over all molecules and using isotropy,

P=\frac{F}{L^2}=\frac{m}{L^3}\sum_{i=1}^N v_{x,i}^2 =\frac{Nm}{V}\left\langle v_x^2\right\rangle =\frac{Nm}{3V}\left\langle v^2\right\rangle

Hence

PV=\frac13Nm\left\langle v^2\right\rangle =\frac23N\left\langle K_{\mathrm{tr}}\right\rangle \qquad{(6)}

Here K_{\mathrm{tr}}=\tfrac12mv^2 is the translational kinetic energy of one molecule.

Comparing Equation 6 with Equation 4 gives the microscopic meaning of temperature:

\left\langle K_{\mathrm{tr}}\right\rangle =\frac12m\left\langle v^2\right\rangle =\frac32k_{\mathrm B}T

The root-mean-square speed is therefore

v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\left\langle v^2\right\rangle} =\sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm B}T}{m}} =\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}},

where M=N_{\mathrm A}m is the molar mass.

Equipartition

Each active quadratic energy term contributes

\left\langle E_{\mathrm{term}}\right\rangle=\frac12k_{\mathrm B}T

For f active terms per molecule,

U=\frac f2Nk_{\mathrm B}T=\frac f2nRT \qquad{(7)}

Examples:

  • Monatomic molecule: three translational terms, so f=3.
  • Rigid linear molecule: three translational and two rotational terms, so f=5 when rotation is active.
  • Each active vibrational mode adds two terms: one kinetic and one potential.

Limits:

  • Equipartition is a classical high-temperature result.
  • A mode freezes out when k_{\mathrm B}T is small relative to its quantum energy spacing.

Molar Heat Capacity

The constant-volume and constant-pressure molar heat capacities are

C_V\equiv\frac1n\left(\frac{\delta Q}{\mathrm dT}\right)_V, \quad C_P\equiv\frac1n\left(\frac{\delta Q}{\mathrm dT}\right)_P

At constant volume, \delta Q_V=\mathrm dU, so for an ideal gas,

C_V = \frac1n\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V \overset{\href{#eq:ideal-gas-internal-energy}{\text{(7)}}}{=} \frac f2R

At constant pressure, Equation 5 and P\,\mathrm dV=nR\,\mathrm dT give

\delta Q_P=\mathrm dU+P\,\mathrm dV =nC_V\,\mathrm dT+nR\,\mathrm dT =n(C_V+R)\,\mathrm dT

Therefore

C_P-C_V=R, \quad \gamma\equiv\frac{C_P}{C_V}

The dimensionless ratio \gamma is called the adiabatic index.

Gas model f C_V C_P \gamma
Monatomic 3 3R/2 5R/2 5/3
Rigid diatomic 5 5R/2 7R/2 7/5

Adiabatic Process

For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas with constant molar heat capacities and only PV work, \delta Q=0 and Equation 5 gives \mathrm dU=-P\,\mathrm dV. Using \mathrm dU=nC_V\,\mathrm dT and P=nRT/V from Equation 4,

\begin{aligned} & nC_V\,\mathrm dT=-\frac{nRT}{V}\,\mathrm dV \\ \implies & \frac{\mathrm dT}{T}=-(\gamma-1)\frac{\mathrm dV}{V} \\ \implies & \int_{T_i}^{T}\frac{\mathrm dT'}{T'} =-(\gamma-1)\int_{V_i}^{V}\frac{\mathrm dV'}{V'} \\ \implies & \ln\frac{T}{T_i}=-(\gamma-1)\ln\frac{V}{V_i} \\ \implies & TV^{\gamma-1}=T_iV_i^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant} \end{aligned}

Combining this result with Equation 4 yields the equivalent forms

\boxed{PV^\gamma=\text{constant}}, \quad T^\gamma P^{1-\gamma}=\text{constant} \qquad{(8)}

The work done by the gas between two states is

W=-\Delta U=nC_V(T_i-T_f) =\frac{P_iV_i-P_fV_f}{\gamma-1}

Ideal-Gas Processes

For a closed ideal-gas system doing only PV work:

Process Constraint Consequence
Isochoric V=\text{constant} W=0, so \Delta U=Q
Isobaric P=\text{constant} W=P(V_f-V_i)
Adiabatic Q=0 \Delta U=-W
Isothermal T=\text{constant} \Delta U=0, so Q=W
Cyclic final state = initial state \Delta U=0, so Q_{\mathrm{net}}=W_{\mathrm{net}}

Figure 4 shows the four noncyclic paths; the gray dashed curves are isotherms.

For a quasistatic isothermal process, Equation 7 gives \Delta U=0, while Equation 4 gives P=nRT/V. Hence

W=\int_{V_i}^{V_f}\frac{nRT}{V}\,\mathrm dV=nRT\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}, \quad Q=W

Speed Distribution

Deriving the Maxwell distribution requires more advanced statistical mechanics, so only its main results are stated here.

At equilibrium, the Maxwell speed distribution for molecules of mass m is

p(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_{\mathrm B}T}\right)^{3/2} v^2\exp\left(-\frac{mv^2}{2k_{\mathrm B}T}\right), \quad \int_0^\infty p(v)\,\mathrm dv=1

The most probable, mean, and root-mean-square speeds are

v_{\mathrm{mp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2k_{\mathrm B}T}{m}}, \quad \langle v\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{8k_{\mathrm B}T}{\pi m}}, \quad v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm B}T}{m}}

  • v_{\mathrm{mp}}<\langle v\rangle<v_{\mathrm{rms}}.
  • Higher T broadens the distribution and shifts its peak to higher speed.

Second Law

Heat Engines

Heat engines exchange energy with thermal reservoirs. A thermal reservoir is an idealized body that can absorb or release energy without a noticeable change in temperature.

A heat engine operates cyclically:

  • absorbs Q_h from a hot reservoir;
  • rejects Q_c to a cold reservoir;
  • delivers work W.

Here Q_h, Q_c, and W are positive magnitudes. Figure 5 shows their directions.

Because the working substance returns to its initial state, \Delta U=0 over one cycle. Equation 5 gives

W=Q_h-Q_c \qquad{(9)}

The thermal efficiency is the fraction of the absorbed energy converted to work:

\boxed{\eta=\frac{W}{Q_h}=1-\frac{Q_c}{Q_h}}

Refrigerators

A refrigerator reverses the heat-engine transfers:

  • removes Q_c from a cold region;
  • receives work W;
  • rejects Q_h=Q_c+W to a warm region.

Its coefficient of performance is

\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm R}=\frac{Q_c}{W}

A heat pump uses the same transfers but measures the energy delivered to the warm region:

\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{HP}}=\frac{Q_h}{W} =\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm R}+1

Statements

The second law restricts the direction of processes allowed by the first law:

  • Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic engine converts heat from one reservoir completely into work.
  • Clausius: no cyclic device transfers heat from cold to hot without work input.

The statements are equivalent: violating either one permits a device that violates the other.

Reversibility

  • Reversible: reversal leaves no net change in the system or surroundings.
  • Necessary conditions: the system remains near equilibrium and no energy is dissipated.
  • Irreversible effects: friction, viscosity, inelastic deformation, free expansion, and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference.
  • Limit: reversible processes set the maximum work and efficiency of real processes.

Carnot Cycle

A Carnot engine operates reversibly between reservoirs at absolute temperatures T_h>T_c. For an ideal-gas working substance with constant C_V:

Process Path Q W \Delta U=Q-W
A\to B Isothermal expansion at T_h Q_h Q_h 0
B\to C Adiabatic expansion; T_h\to T_c 0 nC_V(T_h-T_c) -nC_V(T_h-T_c)
C\to D Isothermal compression at T_c -Q_c -Q_c 0
D\to A Adiabatic compression; T_c\to T_h 0 -nC_V(T_h-T_c) nC_V(T_h-T_c)

Figure 6 shows the cycle. The clockwise enclosed area is the net work per cycle.

At fixed T, Equation 7 gives \Delta U=0. Equations 5 and 4 then give

\begin{aligned} Q_h &=W_{A\to B} =\int_{V_A}^{V_B}\frac{nRT_h}{V}\,\mathrm dV =nRT_h\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}, \\ Q_c &=-W_{C\to D} =-\int_{V_C}^{V_D}\frac{nRT_c}{V}\,\mathrm dV =nRT_c\ln\frac{V_C}{V_D} \end{aligned}

The two adiabatic processes satisfy Equation 8:

T_hV_B^{\gamma-1}=T_cV_C^{\gamma-1}, \quad T_cV_D^{\gamma-1}=T_hV_A^{\gamma-1}

These relations give V_C/V_B=V_D/V_A, or V_B/V_A=V_C/V_D. Therefore

\frac{Q_c}{Q_h} =\frac{T_c\ln(V_C/V_D)}{T_h\ln(V_B/V_A)} =\frac{T_c}{T_h} \qquad{(10)}

The Carnot efficiency is consequently

\eta_{\mathrm C} =\frac{W}{Q_h} \overset{\href{#eq:heat-engine-work}{\text{(9)}}}{=} \frac{Q_h-Q_c}{Q_h} =1-\frac{Q_c}{Q_h} =\boxed{1-\frac{T_c}{T_h}} \qquad{(11)}

Carnot’s theorem states:

  • no engine between T_h and T_c exceeds reversible efficiency;
  • all reversible engines between those temperatures have the same efficiency;
  • \eta_{\mathrm C} is independent of the working substance.

Entropy

For a reversible Carnot cycle:

\oint_{A\to B\to C\to D\to A}\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} =\frac{Q_h}{T_h}+0-\frac{Q_c}{T_c}+0 \overset{\href{#eq:carnot-heat-temperature-ratio}{\text{(10)}}}{=}0.

A smooth reversible cycle can be represented, in the limiting sense, as a collection of infinitesimal Carnot cycles. Contributions along shared paths cancel, leaving only the outer cycle. Thus every reversible cycle satisfies

\boxed{ \oint_{\text{reversible cycle}} \frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}=0 }.

If reversible paths A and B both connect equilibrium states i and f, following A forward and B backward forms a reversible cycle, so

0 =\oint_{A-B}\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} =\int_A\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} -\int_B\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} \implies \int_A\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T} =\int_B\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}.

The path-independent integral defines the state function entropy S, up to an additive constant; see Gradient Field:

\Delta S=S_f-S_i\equiv\int_i^f\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}, \quad \boxed{\mathrm dS=\frac{\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}}.

Here \mathrm dS is an exact differential of a state function, whereas \delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}} is a path-dependent heat transfer; division by the absolute temperature T makes its reversible integral path-independent.

  • SI unit: \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.
  • Entropy is extensive: doubling the system doubles S.
Entropy Change

For an ideal gas, Equation 5 gives \delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}=\mathrm dU+P\,\mathrm dV, so

\mathrm dS=nC_V\frac{\mathrm dT}{T}+nR\frac{\mathrm dV}{V}

If the molar heat capacities are constant, integration yields

\Delta S =nC_V\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}+nR\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i} =nC_P\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}-nR\ln\frac{P_f}{P_i} \qquad{(12)}

For a reversible phase change at constant temperature,

\Delta S=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{rev}}}{T}=\frac{mL}{T},

with the sign reversed for the opposite phase change.

Entropy Production

For a closed system, the entropy balance is

\Delta S=\int_i^f\frac{\delta Q}{T_b}+S_{\mathrm{gen}},

where T_b is the boundary temperature at each heat transfer and S_{\mathrm{gen}} is entropy produced inside the system.

Consider heat Q transferred within an isolated composite from a hot reservoir at T_h to a cold reservoir at T_c<T_h. The reservoirs’ entropy changes give

S_{\mathrm{gen}} =\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} =-\frac{Q}{T_h}+\frac{Q}{T_c} =Q\left(\frac{1}{T_c}-\frac{1}{T_h}\right)>0.

For fixed Q, S_{\mathrm{gen}}\to0 as T_h\to T_c, the reversible limit. A negative value would instead correspond to heat passing from cold to hot without work input, violating the Clausius statement of the second law.

More generally, the second law requires

\boxed{S_{\mathrm{gen}}\geq0},

with equality for a reversible process and strict inequality for an irreversible process.

For a cycle, \Delta S=0, so the entropy balance gives the Clausius inequality:

0=\oint\frac{\delta Q}{T_b}+S_{\mathrm{gen}} \implies \boxed{\oint\frac{\delta Q}{T_b}=-S_{\mathrm{gen}}\leq0}.

If the boundary encloses both the system and its surroundings, the composite is isolated, so \delta Q=0 and

\boxed{ \Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} =\Delta S_{\mathrm{system}}+\Delta S_{\mathrm{surroundings}} =S_{\mathrm{gen}}\geq0 }.

Entropy generation also measures lost work. Compare processes with the same initial and final states and the same environmental constraints. The reversible process generates no entropy and delivers the maximum work. If the environment is a thermal reservoir at uniform temperature T_0, then

\boxed{ W_{\mathrm{lost}} =W_{\mathrm{rev}}-W_{\mathrm{actual}} =T_0S_{\mathrm{gen}} }.

Here S_{\mathrm{gen}} is the total entropy generated by the system and its surroundings. Energy is conserved; irreversibility reduces the part of that energy that can be converted into work.

Microstates

If a macrostate is compatible with \Omega microscopic states of equal probability, Boltzmann’s entropy is

\boxed{S=k_{\mathrm B}\ln\Omega}

For independent systems, \Omega_{AB}=\Omega_A\Omega_B, so the logarithm makes entropy additive:

S_{AB}=k_{\mathrm B}\ln(\Omega_A\Omega_B)=S_A+S_B

An isolated macroscopic system evolves toward overwhelmingly more numerous macrostates, not necessarily toward greater visual disorder.

Oscillations

Simple Harmonic Motion

Any sufficiently regular periodic motion can be represented as a superposition of harmonic components. In simple harmonic motion, the net force is proportional to and opposite the displacement from equilibrium.

Figure 7 shows a block of mass m attached to a spring on a frictionless horizontal surface.

m \ddot x = -kx

The general solution is

x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi), \quad \omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},

where A is the amplitude and \phi is the initial phase. Normalizing each function by its amplitude makes the phase shifts explicit:

\begin{aligned} \frac{x(t)}{A} &=\cos(\omega t+\phi), \\ \frac{v(t)}{A\omega} &=\cos\left(\omega t+\phi+\frac{\pi}{2}\right), \\ \frac{a(t)}{A\omega^2} &=\cos(\omega t+\phi+\pi) =-\frac{x(t)}{A}. \end{aligned}

Figure 8 compares the three normalized functions over one cycle.

With \theta=\omega t+\phi, eliminating the phase between x=A\cos\theta and v=-A\omega\sin\theta gives

v^2=A^2\omega^2\sin^2\theta=A^2\omega^2\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)=\omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right).

Using m\omega^2=k and taking the spring potential energy to be zero at equilibrium,

\begin{aligned} U&=\frac12kx^2, \\ K&=\frac12mv^2=\frac12k\left(A^2-x^2\right), \\ E&=K+U=\frac12kA^2=\frac12m\omega^2A^2. \end{aligned}

In the ideal frictionless system, E remains constant: energy alternates between kinetic energy at equilibrium and spring potential energy at the turning points.

Simple harmonic motion is the projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter: a point moving on a circle of radius A at angular speed \omega projects onto x=A\cos(\omega t+\phi).

Waves

Waves on a String

Basics

A wave field describes a disturbance distributed through space and time. A traveling wave propagates and can transport energy; a standing wave has a fixed spatial pattern and, in the ideal case, no net energy transport. In a mechanical wave, elements of the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions rather than traveling with the disturbance.

A wave is transverse when the material moves at right angles to the direction of travel. It is longitudinal when the material moves in the same direction as the wave.

For a wave on a string, x labels the equilibrium position of a small piece of string, and y(x,t) is its vertical displacement. The wave speed tells how fast the shape moves along the string. The velocity \partial y/\partial t tells how fast one piece of string moves up or down.

Traveling Wave

Let y(x,0)=F(x) describe the wave shape at t=0. If the whole shape moves to the right at speed v without changing, then

y(x,t)=F(x-vt).

A left-moving wave has the form

y(x,t)=G(x+vt).

To check how this function changes, let \xi=x-vt. Since \partial\xi/\partial x=1 and \partial\xi/\partial t=-v, the chain rule gives

\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} &=\frac{\partial F}{\partial\xi}, & \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2} &=\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial\xi^2}, \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} &=-v\frac{\partial F}{\partial\xi}, & \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} &=v^2\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial\xi^2}. \end{aligned}

Therefore, any wave shape that moves unchanged at speed v satisfies

\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} =v^2\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}. \qquad{(13)}

The same equation holds for the left-moving wave G(x+vt). Its first time derivative has the opposite sign, but the second derivative does not.

Sine Wave

A sine wave with amplitude A, wavelength \lambda, and starting phase \phi can be written at t=0 as

F(x)=A\sin(kx+\phi), \quad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}.

Substituting this shape into the right-moving form y(x,t)=F(x-vt) gives

y(x,t) =A\sin\left(k(x-vt)+\phi\right) =A\sin(kx-kvt+\phi).

At a fixed position, one period T changes the phase by 2\pi, so kvT=2\pi. Define

f=\frac{1}{T}, \quad \omega=2\pi f=kv,

the wave becomes

y(x,t)=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi), \quad v=\frac{\omega}{k}=\lambda f.

Its phase is \theta(x,t)=kx-\omega t+\phi.

At a Fixed Position

Keeping x=x_0 fixed means following the same piece of string. Its displacement and vertical velocity are

\begin{aligned} y(x_0,t) &=A\sin(kx_0-\omega t+\phi), \\ u_y(x_0,t) &=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}(x_0,t) =-A\omega\cos(kx_0-\omega t+\phi). \end{aligned}

Each piece of string therefore moves in simple harmonic motion with angular frequency \omega. Its label x_0 stays fixed while the piece moves in the y direction.

At a Fixed Phase

A crest has fixed phase:

\theta(x,t)=kx-\omega t+\phi =\frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi n,

Keeping n fixed follows one particular crest:

x_n(t) =\frac{\omega t-\phi+\frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi n}{k} =x_n(0)+vt.

Figure 9 contrasts the moving crest with a fixed string element.

Wave Equation for a String

Consider an ideal string under uniform tension F_T, with linear mass density \mu={\mathrm dm} / {\mathrm dx}.

Figure 10 isolates the short piece of string between two string elements whose equilibrium positions are x and x+\Delta x. At each endpoint, the tension acts tangent to the string and pulls away from the element.

Let \theta_1 and \theta_2 be the signed tangent angles at the two endpoints. For small slopes, \cos\theta_i\simeq1 and \sin\theta_i\simeq\tan\theta_i. Thus the horizontal tension components cancel to first order,

F_x=F_T(\cos\theta_2-\cos\theta_1)\simeq0,

The net vertical force is

\begin{aligned} F_y &=F_T(\sin\theta_2-\sin\theta_1) \\ &\simeq F_T\left[ \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(x+\Delta x,t) -\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(x,t) \right] \\ &\simeq F_T \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}(x,t)\Delta x, \end{aligned}

where the last step is a first-order expansion in \Delta x.

Then:

ma = F \implies \mu\Delta x\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} = F_T\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}\Delta x \implies \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{F_T}{\mu} \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2} \overset{\href{#eq:traveling-wave-relation}{\text{(13)}}}{\implies} \boxed{ v=\sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}} } \qquad{(14)}

Thus the wave speed depends on the string tension and linear density, not on the shape of the wave.

Energy and Power

A short piece \mathrm dx has vertical velocity \partial y/\partial t, so its kinetic energy is

\mathrm dK =\frac12\mu \left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\right)^2\mathrm dx.

For a gentle slope, its increase in length is

\mathrm ds-\mathrm dx =\left[ \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right)^2}-1 \right]\mathrm dx \simeq \frac12\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right)^2\mathrm dx.

This stretching stores elastic potential energy:

\mathrm dU=F_T(\mathrm ds-\mathrm dx) \simeq\frac12F_T \left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right)^2\mathrm dx.

For a sine wave on the string, Equation 14 gives

v^2= \frac{\omega^2}{k^2} =\frac{F_T}{\mu} \implies F_Tk^2=\mu\omega^2.

Using this relation for y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi) gives equal kinetic and potential energy densities:

\frac{\mathrm dK}{\mathrm dx} =\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dx} =\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2 \cos^2(kx-\omega t+\phi).

Adding both forms of energy over one wavelength at a fixed time gives

E_\lambda =K_\lambda+U_\lambda =\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2\lambda

Cut the string at position x and consider the part to its right. In the small-slope model, the part to the left exerts transverse force F_y on it, while the point at the cut has transverse velocity u_y:

F_y=-F_T\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \quad u_y=\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}.

Thus the power crossing the cut toward increasing x is the rate at which the left part does work on the right part:

\mathcal P(x,t) =F_yu_y =-F_T\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}. \qquad{(15)}

For the right-moving sine wave, the average over one period is

\boxed{ \overline{\mathcal P} =\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2v }.

Sound Waves

Sound in a fluid is a longitudinal wave in which fluid elements oscillate along the direction of propagation, producing pressure variations.

Sound Wave Equation

Homogeneous Fluid

Consider a plane sound wave traveling along x through a homogeneous fluid with equilibrium pressure P_0, density \rho, and bulk modulus B from Equation 3. Let s(x,t) be the displacement of the fluid element whose equilibrium position is x.

Figure 11 shows this element in equilibrium and during the wave, together with the pressure forces.

A fluid section with equilibrium length \mathrm dx and cross-sectional area A_c has equilibrium volume \mathrm dV=A_c\,\mathrm dx and volume change

\delta V=A_c\left[s(x+\mathrm dx,t)-s(x,t)\right]\simeq A_c\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\,\mathrm dx.

Thus \delta V/\mathrm dV\simeq\partial s/\partial x, and Equation 3 gives

\Delta p =-B\frac{\delta V}{\mathrm dV} =-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x} \qquad{(16)}

Since P=P_0+\Delta p with uniform P_0, \partial P/\partial x=\partial\Delta p/\partial x. The opposing pressure forces on the two faces give

\begin{aligned} F_x &=A_c\left[P(x,t)-P(x+\mathrm dx,t)\right] \\ &\simeq-A_c\frac{\partial\Delta p}{\partial x}\,\mathrm dx \\ &=BA_c\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2}\,\mathrm dx. \end{aligned}

The section has mass \mathrm dm=\rho A_c\,\mathrm dx. Newton’s second law gives

\rho A_c\,\mathrm dx\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial t^2} =BA_c\,\mathrm dx\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2} \implies \frac{\partial^2s}{\partial t^2} =\frac{B}{\rho}\frac{\partial^2s}{\partial x^2}.

Comparison with Equation 13 gives

\boxed{ v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}} }. \qquad{(17)}

Like the string result in Equation 14, the numerator (B or F_T) measures restoring strength and the denominator (\rho or \mu) measures inertia.

Ideal Gas

In an ideal gas, sound propagation is treated as an adiabatic process because compression and expansion occur too rapidly for appreciable heat exchange.

Equation 4 gives PV=nRT_{\mathrm K}. For the reversible adiabatic changes derived in Equation 8, PV^\gamma=C; the subscript S below denotes constant entropy:

% \ln P+\gamma\ln V= 0 \implies \frac{\mathrm dP}{P} = -\gamma\frac{\mathrm dV}{V} % \implies \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_S = -\gamma\frac{P}{V} \implies \left.\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_S\right|_0 =-\gamma\frac{P_0}{V_0}

Then from Equation 3:

B =-V_0\left.\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_S\right|_0 =-V_0\left(-\gamma\frac{P_0}{V_0}\right) =\gamma P_0. \qquad{(18)}

Then:

v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}} \overset{\href{#eq:adiabatic-bulk-modulus}{\text{(18)}}}{=}\sqrt{\gamma\frac{P_0}{\rho}} =\sqrt{\gamma\frac{nRT_{\mathrm K}/V_0}{nM/V_0}} =\sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T_{\mathrm K}}{M}}.

Here \gamma is the heat-capacity ratio, R is the universal gas constant, M is the molar mass.

For dry air near ordinary atmospheric conditions:

v\simeq(331\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}) \sqrt{\frac{T_{\mathrm K}}{273.15\,\mathrm{K}}}.

Sine Sound Wave

For a right-moving sound wave with a sine shape, write the displacement as

s(x,t)=s_{\max}\cos(kx-\omega t+\phi), \quad v=\frac{\omega}{k}.

The velocity u of one fluid part along the tube is

u(x,t)=\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} =\omega s_{\max}\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi).

Using Equation 16, the pressure change is

\begin{aligned} \Delta p(x,t) &=-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x} \\ &=Bk s_{\max}\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi) \\ &=\rho v\omega s_{\max}\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi). \end{aligned}

Therefore,

\boxed{ \Delta p_{\max}=\rho v\omega s_{\max} }.

Figure 12 compares displacement, pressure change, and fluid velocity after each is divided by its maximum value.

Energy, Power, and Intensity

Like a wave on a string, a sound wave carries kinetic and elastic potential energy; here the elastic energy is stored in compression rather than stretching. The corresponding energy densities are

\frac{\mathrm dK}{\mathrm dV} =\frac12\rho \left(\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}\right)^2, \quad \frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dV} =\frac12B \left(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\right)^2 =\frac{(\Delta p)^2}{2B}.

Equation 17 and v=\omega/k give Bk^2=\rho\omega^2, so the right-moving sine wave has equal kinetic and stored energy per unit volume:

\frac{\mathrm dK}{\mathrm dV} =\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dV} =\frac12\rho\omega^2s_{\max}^2 \sin^2(kx-\omega t+\phi).

At any fixed time, adding the energy over one wavelength in a tube of cross-sectional area A_c gives

K_\lambda=U_\lambda =\frac14\rho A_c\omega^2s_{\max}^2\lambda, \quad E_\lambda =\frac12\rho A_c\omega^2s_{\max}^2\lambda.

The power crossing A_c at time t is the pressure force times the fluid velocity:

\mathcal P(x,t)=A_c\,\Delta p(x,t)u(x,t).

For the right-moving sine wave, averaging over one period gives

\overline{\mathcal P} =\frac12\rho A_c v\omega^2s_{\max}^2.

Sound intensity is average power per unit area:

\boxed{ I=\frac{\overline{\mathcal P}}{A_c} =\frac12\rho v\omega^2s_{\max}^2 =\frac{(\Delta p_{\max})^2}{2\rho v} }.

Human hearing covers a very wide range of sound intensities, so sound level uses a logarithm:

\boxed{ \beta=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)\,\mathrm{dB} }, \quad I_0=1.00 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.

Sound Doppler Effect

1-D Motion

Sound speed is measured relative to the fluid. Figure 13 assumes one-dimensional motion and takes u_S and u_O as positive when the source and observer move toward each other.

This forward-wave derivation assumes u_S<v.

For T_S=1/f_S,

\lambda'=vT_S-u_ST_S =\frac{v-u_S}{f_S}.

The observer meets the wavefronts at relative speed v+u_O. Thus the time between successive wavefront arrivals is T_O, where

T_O=\frac{\lambda'}{v+u_O}\implies f_O=\frac{1}{T_O}=\frac{v+u_O}{\lambda'}=\frac{v+u_O}{(v-u_S)/f_S}=\boxed{f_S\frac{v+u_O}{v-u_S}}

Motion toward each other raises the observed frequency; motion apart lowers it.

Motion in Any Direction

For motion not restricted to one dimension, let \hat n point along the ray from the source at emission to the observer at reception, and let \vec u_S and \vec u_O be their velocities relative to the fluid. Figure 14 shows their projections along \hat n.

Replacing the collinear speeds by their signed components along \hat n gives

\boxed{ f_O=f_S\frac{v-\vec u_O\cdot\hat n}{v-\vec u_S\cdot\hat n} }

In the collinear case above, \vec u_S\cdot\hat n=u_S and \vec u_O\cdot\hat n=-u_O, recovering the one-dimensional result.

For speeds small compared with v,

\frac{f_O-f_S}{f_S} =\frac{(\vec u_S-\vec u_O)\cdot\hat n}{v-\vec u_S\cdot\hat n} \simeq\frac{(\vec u_S-\vec u_O)\cdot\hat n}{v}

Supersonic Source

If a source moves faster than sound, v_S\equiv|\vec u_S|>v, its spherical wavefronts form a Mach cone. Figure 15 shows how the edges of the wavefronts form this cone.

After time t, the source has traveled v_St while a wavefront has radius vt. The cone half-angle \theta therefore satisfies

\boxed{ \sin\theta=\frac{vt}{v_St}=\frac{v}{v_S}=\frac{1}{\mathcal M} },

where \mathcal M=v_S/v is the Mach number.

Superposition

Superposition applies to the same physical field governed by the same linear equation. For

\begin{aligned} \mathcal L[y] &\equiv\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2} -v^2\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}, \\ \mathcal L[y_1]=\mathcal L[y_2]=0 &\implies \mathcal L[c_1y_1+c_2y_2] \\ &=c_1\mathcal L[y_1]+c_2\mathcal L[y_2] \\ &=0. \end{aligned}

Thus c_1y_1+c_2y_2 is also a solution: wave fields add pointwise even when their amplitudes, frequencies, phases, or directions differ. The string and sound models above are linear only under the small-slope and small-amplitude approximations, respectively.

The principle does not permit adding different physical fields, such as string displacement and sound pressure, into one field. It also does not generally apply to nonlinear wave equations. Energy and intensity do not add like the field because they are quadratic; for any Q[y]\propto y^2,

Q[y_1+y_2]\propto y_1^2+y_2^2+2y_1y_2,

so Q[y_1+y_2]\ne Q[y_1]+Q[y_2] unless the cross term vanishes, possibly after averaging.

Interference

For two waves with the same k and \omega, let \vartheta=kx-\omega t and let \delta be their phase difference:

y_1=A_1\sin\vartheta,\quad y_2=A_2\sin(\vartheta+\delta)

Their sum is another sine wave with the same k and \omega:

y_1+y_2=(A_1+A_2\cos\delta)\sin\vartheta+A_2\sin\delta\cos\vartheta=A_R\sin(\vartheta+\phi)

Matching the sine and cosine coefficients gives

A_R^2=(A_1+A_2\cos\delta)^2+(A_2\sin\delta)^2=A_1^2+A_2^2+2A_1A_2\cos\delta

For equal amplitudes A_1=A_2=A,

A_R=2A\left|\cos\frac{\delta}{2}\right|,\quad \delta=2\pi m\implies A_R=2A,\quad \delta=(2m+1)\pi\implies A_R=0

The first case is constructive interference; the second is destructive interference.

Beats

At a fixed position, two equal-amplitude waves with nearby angular frequencies \omega_1 and \omega_2 give

y=A\cos\omega_1t+A\cos\omega_2t=2A\cos\left(\frac{\omega_1-\omega_2}{2}t\right)\cos\left(\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}t\right)

The fast oscillation occurs at the average frequency, while the slowly varying factor produces the amplitude envelope. Successive envelope maxima are separated by

T_{\mathrm{beat}}=\frac{2\pi}{|\omega_1-\omega_2|}\implies \boxed{f_{\mathrm{beat}}=|f_1-f_2|}

For the example in Figure 16, let f_1=10\,\mathrm{Hz} and f_2=12\,\mathrm{Hz}. Since \omega=2\pi f,

\frac{y}{A}=\cos(20\pi t)+\cos(24\pi t)=2\cos(2\pi t)\cos(22\pi t)

The fast factor has frequency 11\,\mathrm{Hz}, while the envelope reaches a maximum every T_{\mathrm{beat}}=0.50\,\mathrm{s}, corresponding to f_{\mathrm{beat}}=2\,\mathrm{Hz}.

Standing Waves

Formation and Properties

Consider two waves with the same amplitude, wavelength, and frequency traveling in opposite directions:

y_R=A\sin(kx-\omega t),\quad y_L=A\sin(kx+\omega t)

Superposition and the sine addition identity give

y=y_R+y_L=A\sin(kx-\omega t)+A\sin(kx+\omega t)=\boxed{2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)} \qquad{(19)}

The factor \cos(\omega t) describes simple harmonic motion in time. The position-dependent amplitude is

A_{\mathrm{standing}}(x)=2A|\sin(kx)|

Figure 17 shows that the shape oscillates between opposite extremes without traveling along the medium.

Nodes have zero amplitude:

\sin\left(kx_n^{(\mathrm{node})}\right)=0\implies kx_n^{(\mathrm{node})}=n\pi\implies \boxed{x_n^{(\mathrm{node})}=\frac{n\lambda}{2}},\; n\in\mathbb Z

Antinodes have maximum amplitude 2A:

\begin{aligned} \left|\sin\left(kx_n^{(\mathrm{antinode})}\right)\right|=1 &\implies kx_n^{(\mathrm{antinode})}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2} \\ &\implies \boxed{x_n^{(\mathrm{antinode})}=\frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{4}}, \quad n\in\mathbb Z \end{aligned}

Points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase; neighboring intervals have a phase difference of \pi.

Substituting the total standing wave in Equation 19 into Equation 15:

\begin{aligned} \mathcal P(x,t) &=-F_T\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t} \\ &=F_TA^2k\omega\sin(2kx)\sin(2\omega t), \\ \overline{\mathcal P}(x) &=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T\mathcal P(x,t)\,\mathrm dt=0. \end{aligned}

Thus the instantaneous power is nonzero at generic x and t, but vanishes at every node and antinode and whenever t=nT/4, n\in\mathbb Z. Its sign reverses during each cycle, so no net energy crosses any fixed point over one period.

Normal Modes

Theory

Boundary conditions restrict a finite wave system to discrete standing-wave shapes and frequencies, each defining a normal mode.

Seek a solution whose spatial and temporal parts factor as y(x,t)=X(x)T(t). Since X depends only on x and T only on t,

\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2}=X(x)T''(t), \quad \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}=X''(x)T(t).

Substitute these derivatives into Equation 13:

\underbrace{X(x)T''(t)}_{\partial^2y/\partial t^2} =v^2 \underbrace{X''(x)T(t)}_{\partial^2y/\partial x^2} \implies \frac{T''(t)}{v^2T(t)}=\frac{X''(x)}{X(x)}.

The left side depends only on t and the right side only on x. For them to be equal for every x and t, both must equal the same constant. For oscillatory normal modes, write this constant as -k^2, with k>0:

\frac{T''(t)}{v^2T(t)}=\frac{X''(x)}{X(x)}=-k^2.

The spatial and temporal factors therefore satisfy

X''+k^2X=0,\quad T''+\omega^2T=0,\quad \omega=vk

These differential equations have oscillatory solutions for any k, but the solution must also satisfy the constraints at the ends of the string. Figure 18 contrasts fixed and transversely free ends.

At a fixed end x=x_e, the endpoint cannot move, so its displacement must vanish at all times. For a nonzero T(t),

y(x_e,t)=X(x_e)T(t)=0 \implies \boxed{X(x_e)=0}.

At an ideal transversely free end, the support exerts no transverse force. In the small-slope model, the transverse component of tension is proportional to the endpoint slope; its sign depends on which end is considered:

F_y\simeq\pm F_T\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=0 \implies \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}(x_e,t)=X'(x_e)T(t)=0 \implies \boxed{X'(x_e)=0}.

Only certain values k_n allow a nonzero spatial shape X_n(x) to satisfy the required conditions at both ends. Each such shape and its frequency \omega_n=vk_n form a normal mode.

Case Study

String fixed at both ends. For a string of length L fixed at x=0 and x=L, the general spatial solution is

X(x)=C\sin(kx)+D\cos(kx)

Applying both boundary conditions gives

X(0)=0\implies D=0,\quad X(L)=0\implies C\sin(kL)=0

A nonzero mode requires

\sin(kL)=0\implies k_nL=n\pi\implies \boxed{k_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}},\quad n=1,2,3,\ldots

Hence the allowed wavelengths and frequencies are

\lambda_n=\frac{2\pi}{k_n}=\frac{2L}{n},\quad f_n=\frac{v}{\lambda_n}=\frac{nv}{2L}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}},\quad \omega_n=2\pi f_n=\frac{n\pi v}{L} \qquad{(20)}

The mode number n counts the number of half-wavelengths that fit along the string. The n=1 mode has the lowest nonzero frequency f_1=v/(2L) and is called the fundamental, or first harmonic. The modes n=2,3,\ldots have frequencies f_n=nf_1 and are the higher harmonics. Figure 19 shows the first three modes.

Each mode has the form

y_n(x,t)=A_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(\omega_nt+\phi_n)

Because the wave equation is linear, the most general motion of the ideal fixed string is a superposition of its normal modes:

y(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(\omega_nt+\phi_n)

Other Systems

Air columns. For the longitudinal air displacement s, a closed end is a displacement node, s=0. At an open end, \Delta p\simeq0, so Equation 16 gives \partial s/\partial x\simeq0, a displacement antinode. The ideal natural frequencies are

\begin{aligned} f_n&=\frac{nv}{2L} &&\text{open--open or closed--closed}, \\ f_n&=\frac{(2n-1)v}{4L} &&\text{closed--open}, \end{aligned} \quad n=1,2,3,\ldots

Thus a closed–open tube contains only odd multiples of its fundamental frequency.

Rods. A slender rod with Young’s modulus E and mass density \rho_s supports longitudinal displacement u(x,t) with

\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2} =c_L^2\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}, \quad c_L=\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho_s}}.

A fixed end has u=0; a stress-free end has \partial u/\partial x=0. The nonzero natural frequencies are

\begin{aligned} f_n&=\frac{nc_L}{2L} &&\text{fixed--fixed or free--free}, \\ f_n&=\frac{(2n-1)c_L}{4L} &&\text{fixed--free}, \end{aligned} \quad n=1,2,3,\ldots

A free–free rod also has a zero-frequency rigid-translation mode.

Membranes. For a rectangular membrane of side lengths L_x and L_y, fixed along all four edges and with transverse wave speed c_m, the normal modes have

\begin{aligned} X_{mn}(x,y) &=\sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L_x}\right) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi y}{L_y}\right), \\ f_{mn} &=\frac{c_m}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{L_x}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{n}{L_y}\right)^2}, \quad m,n=1,2,3,\ldots \end{aligned}

Two mode numbers are required because the membrane varies in two spatial directions; its nodes form lines rather than isolated points.

See the Air Columns, Rods, and Membranes for step-by-step derivations.
